messages.subject: release of seewave 1.6.4
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

A new version of seewave (1.6.4) was deposited on CRAN some time ago.
Windows binaries are already ready but Mac binaries are stil in the pipes.

This version requires the installation of the C library libsndfile
(http://www.mega-nerd.com/libsndfile/) easy to install on Linux system,
a bit more tricky on Windows and Mac sytems. I hope you can install it
without any trouble.

Thanks very much to Alicia Stotz, Ethan Brown and Jesse Ross for their
input!

Best regards

Jerome

CHANGES IN SEEWAVE VERSION 1.6.4 [28-June-2012]

NEW FEATURES
     o stft.ext(): a new function to compute externally (i.e. out of R
environment) the short-term Fourier transform. This function has been
developed to speed up computing process time when doing batch analysis.
     o timer(): a new argument, 'tlim', to change to time axis.
     o savewav() : a new argument, 'rescale', to rescale the amplitude
of the exported .wav file.

OTHER CHANGES
     o ama(), dynspec(), spec(), meanspec(), spectro(), spectro3D(): a
small shift in Fourier coefficients fixed.
     o env(): computing the Hilbert envelope should be faster.
     o export(), listen(), savewav(): the sampling frequency can now be
changed with the argument 'f' (i.e. it is now possible to listen or to
write a wav file with a different sampling frequency than the original one).
     o meanspec(): should be slightly faster.
     o noisew(): the argument 'listen' now works properly.
     o timer(): should be faster.
     o Numerous typoes and small errors fixed in the documentation!

messages.subject: Detecting Gerygone in the secondary forest
messages.subject_clean: Detecting Gerygone in the secondary forest
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
First off, thanks for the great R package!

I have done some test recordings with Song Meters in secondary forest in Sumatra. Now I am comparing the performance and usefulness of Song Scope to Seewave for our research. I have been working on it for a while, but I stumble upon a problem:

I want to compare a reference call of 3 seconds to a 100s recording which I know contains 5 other calls of the bird Gerygone sulphurea.

I kept only frequencies between 3500 and 5000 Hz. I use covspectro (corenv never ended) to compare the reference call:

to successive parts of the 100s recording, extracted with cutw. The problem is, the extracted parts look like that:

although in the original spectogram, the parts are white and relatively silent, only containing background noise. I guess the spectrograms use red for the highest amplitude (even if it is low) and color the other sounds relative to the loudest sound.
However, the correlations between my reference call and those background noise parts are highly significant (coef>90%) and the time offset is always 0. There is no way to distinguish really significant correlations (between two real calls) from unsignificant ones (between reference call and background noise). Is there a way to disable the amplitude autoscaling such that comparisons with background noise do not turn out so significant?
I attach my code here:
> rm(list = ls())
> setwd("D:/Burung")
> library(seewave)
> library(tuneR)
> freq=22050
> song<-readWave("original_part.wav")
>
> songf<-resamp(song,f=44100,g=freq,output="Wave")
> songf<-ffilter(songf,from=3500,to=5000,output="Wave")
>
> reff<-cutw(songf,from=10.75,to=13.75,plot=FALSE,output="Wave")
>
> RESU=NULL
> dura=trunc(length(songf)/freq)
> refd=trunc(length(reff)/freq)
> bins<-seq(from=1,to=trunc(dura),by=refd/2)
> pb <- txtProgressBar(min=0,max=max(bins),style=3)
>
> for (i in bins){
>   scan<-cutw(songf,from=i,to=i+refd,output="Wave")
>   resu<-covspectro(reff,scan,f=freq,n=15,plot=FALSE)
>   RESU<-cbind(RESU,resu)
>   Sys.sleep(0.1)
>   setTxtProgressBar(pb,i)
> }
> close(pb)
Am I doing a mistake?
I would like to add that it would be handy if covspectro could compare time waves of different lengths.
Greetings from Sumatra

messages.body_plain:
Hi Peter,

You're passing in your Wave object, LKW0, rather than a vector as it expects.

You could alter your code snippet at the bottom to read

spec <- meanspec(LKW0, plot=FALSE)
roughness(spec)

best,
jesse

messages.subject: Using dBref in meanpec and spec
messages.subject_clean: Using dBref in meanpec and spec
messages.body_plain:
Greetings!
I am using your great package to look at the self noise of an accelerometer and have run into a problem.   Specificallly when I execute

meanspec(raw_data$Ax, f=(f*1000), wl=win_len, dB="max0", dBref=(sens*bw_sqrt) , flab="Frequency(Hz)", alab="Noise dBuG/Hz^0.5")

I get results that are not consistent.  I reviewd the source code in seewave.r and found that the spectral result is being normalized to the max bin
e.g. y3<-y2/max(y2)

If something like
if(is.null(dBref)) y3<-y2/max(y2)
else y3<-y2
were to be implemented when using dBref, then absolute calibrations could be performed.

I edited the source code to try this out, but then my inexperience with building packages stopped me.  When I tried to execute
R CMD build seewave

the following error occurred
Error: processing vignette ‘seewave_IO.rnw’ failed with diagnostics:
 chunk 14
Error in library(sound) : there is no package called ‘sound’

How do I go about getting a changes like this implemented (locally and in the main branch)?

Thanks
Mike

So I fixed my petty compile problems by installing the package sound (appears to only be required for compile?).  And made the above modifications.  I also ran into an issue with the stft function when norm is set to false, the function still normalized the return values, I replaced the offending function with a window length normalization
#  else {z<-z2/max(z2)}
  else {z<-z2/(wl/2)}
which provides the expected response.
Cheers
Mike
